items.bodyEn: Ejiri, the eighteenth post town, is remembered for a sudden wind. In Hokusai's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, 'Ejiri in Suruga Province' catches travellers on a marshy road as a gust bends the reeds, snatches hats and scatters a sheaf of paper, while Fuji stands as a bare outline. The Gust Keeper takes its name from that print.
items.sourceNote: Hokusai, Thirty-six Views of Mt Fuji, 'Ejiri in Suruga Province' (c. 1830–32)

items.bodyEn: Hiroshige drew Ejiri not as a street of inns but as a harbour: 'Ejiri: Distant View of Miho' fills the foreground with boat masts at Shimizu, the port that served Sunpu, and sets the pine grove of Miho no Matsubara on its sand spit across the bay. The town began as a Takeda fortress in 1570.

The grammar word for the passive, ukemi, means 'receiving body', and its first kanji is a hand-off frozen in ink. The oldest forms show one hand above and one below, passing a small boat; the boat later shrank to the flat middle stroke. The Shuowen glosses it as 'mutual handing over', so giver and receiver share one character.
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi, entry 受 (相付也); oracle-bone glyph forms

items.bodyEn: Japanese lets you make an intransitive verb passive to show that something happened to you and you minded: あめにふられた, 'I got rained on'; ともだちにこられて, 'a friend turned up on me'; こどもになかれた, 'the kid cried on me'. English needs a whole clause for this; Japanese does it with られる. Use it for mild grievances, not for neutral reports.
